questions.question: Differentiate Book keeping and Accounting. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Differentiate Book-keeping and Accounting
  • Basis Book-keeping Accounting
  • Meaning Recording of financial transactions systematically. Interpreting, classifying, summarizing, and analyzing financial information.
  • Scope Narrow—limited to recording and maintaining books. Wider—includes analysis, interpretation, and reporting.
  • Objective To maintain accurate and complete records. To determine financial results and position for decision-making.
  • Stage Primary stage of accounting. Secondary stage after book-keeping.
  • Skills
  • required Basic recording skills. Analytical and interpretative skills.
  • Outcome Provides raw financial data. Prepares final accounts and financial statements.
questions.source_exam: First Semester MGU-UGP/MGU-BBA/MGU-BCA Honours Examinations November 2025

questions.question: A business wants to maintain proper records of all cash receipts and payments. Explain how the business can apply the concept of a cash book in recording these transactions. Discuss its features and advantages . / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• A business can maintain a cash book to record all cash receipts and payments on a daily
  • basis. Every time cash is received, it is entered on the debit side, and every time cash is paid, it
  • is entered on the credit side. The cash book acts as both a journal (for recording) and a ledger
  • (for posting) for all cash transactions.

• Double Entry System – Explanation, Advantages, and Limitations
  • Application of Double Entry System:A small business can use the double entry system
  • to record all financial transactions by ensuring that every transaction affects at least two
  • accounts—one debit and one credit.
  • Example: If the business purchases goods for cash: Purchases A/c — Debit,Cash A/c — Credit
  • This ensures that the accounting equation Assets = Liabilities + Capital always remains
  • balanced.

questions.question: A business wants to manage small, frequent cash payments efficiently. Evaluate the role of a petty cash book in handling such transactions. Discuss its advantages and importance. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Role of a Petty Cash Book
  • A Petty Cash Book is used by a business to record small, frequent cash payments such as
  • postage, stationery, refreshments, travel expenses, and minor repairs.
  • Instead of recording every small transaction in the main cash book, the business maintains a
  • separate petty cash system, usually under the imprest system, where a fixed amount is given to
  • the petty cashier for small expenses.The petty cashier records each expense under proper heads
  • (postage, traveling, telephone, etc.) which makes tracking and controlling petty expenses simple
  • and efficient
  • Advantages of a Petty Cash Book
questions.source_exam: First Semester MGU-UGP/MGU-BBA/MGU-BCA Honours Examinations November 2025

questions.question: Differentiate Trading Account and Profit and Loss Account. / [CO3, CO4] [6x5 = 30]
questions.solution_html:
• Difference Between Trading Account and Profit and Loss Account
  • Basis Trading Account Profit and Loss Account
  • Purpose
  • To determine Gross Profit or Gross
  • Loss from buying and selling of
  • goods.
  • To determine Net Profit or Net Loss after
  • considering all indirect incomes and
  • indirect expenses.
  • Focus
  • Deals with direct expenses and
  • direct incomes related to production
  • or purchase of goods.
  • Deals with indirect expenses and indirect
  • incomes related to administration, selling,
  • and financing.
  • Items
  • Included
  • Opening stock, purchases, direct
  • expenses (wages, carriage inwards),
  • sales, closing stock.
  • Salaries, rent, advertising, depreciation,
  • interest, commission, and other indirect
  • items.
  • Stage in Final
  • Accounts
  • Prepared first, before Profit and Loss
  • Account. Prepared after the Trading Account.
  • Result Shown Shows Gross Profit or Gross Loss. Shows Net Profit or Net Loss.
  • Transfer of
  • Balance
  • Gross Profit is transferred to Profit
  • and Loss A/c credit side; Gross Loss
  • to debit side.
  • Net Profit is transferred to Capital A/c (or
  • retained earnings).
  • Nature Measures production and trading efficiency. Measures overall business performance.
  • Period
  • Covered For an accounting period (1 year). Also for the same accounting period.
